prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Traditional Multi-view Clustering (MVC) operates under the static assumption that all views (modalities) are available simultaneously during training. However, in many real-world scenarios—such as medical diagnostics or federated learning—data views are acquired sequentially over time (Continual Multi-view Clustering, or CMVC). Existing solutions typically rely on "late fusion," where separate models are trained for each view and their outputs are averaged. This approach is fundamentally flawed for two reasons: it fails to account for the significant "domain gap" or feature discrepancies between different views, and it struggles with "catastrophic forgetting" because privacy constraints prevent access to historical view data. Furthermore, these methods often treat all incoming data equally, making them highly susceptible to view-specific noise that degrades the consensus clustering.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that CMVC should be reframed not as a simple fusion task, but as a **Domain Adaptation** problem. We believe that instead of training distinct models for every new view, we can maintain a single "base model" that continuously adapts to incoming views. By treating the transition between views as a domain shift, we can employ **self-training** to bridge the feature gap. Furthermore, we posit that **structural alignment**—preserving the geometric relationships between samples rather than the samples themselves—is sufficient to prevent catastrophic forgetting without violating data privacy.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a unified framework, "AdaptCMVC," designed to evolve a single model through sequential data streams. The methodology consists of three logically distinct components:

**1. Generative Base Initialization**
We will begin by establishing a robust feature extraction backbone using the first available view. We intend to use a generative approach (specifically, a Variational Autoencoder structure with input masking) to force the model to learn noise-resilient representations from the start. This creates the "source" domain for our adaptation process.

**2. Noise-Robust Self-Training (The Adaptation Mechanism)**
To adapt this base model to subsequent, divergent views, we will utilize a Teacher-Student framework.
*   **Teacher-Student Setup:** The "Teacher" will be a temporally averaged version of the "Student" model, providing stable target representations for the new view.
*   **Prototype-Based Noise Filtering:** Crucially, we will not treat all guidance from the Teacher as equal. We will carry over "cluster prototypes" (centroids) from the previous session. We will design a loss function that weighs the adaptation updates based on the distance between a sample and these historical prototypes. Samples far from established cluster centers will be treated as noise and their influence on the gradient will be suppressed, ensuring the model only learns from high-confidence data.

**3. Global Structure Alignment (The Anti-Forgetting Mechanism)**
To prevent the model from forgetting previous clustering structures when adapting to the new view, we will implement a regularization strategy that does not require storing raw data.
*   **Similarity Matrix Maintenance:** We will maintain a global similarity matrix that records the pairwise relationships between samples.
*   **Alignment Objective:** As the model processes a new view, we will enforce a consistency constraint where the pairwise similarities in the *current* feature space must align with the historical similarity matrix (updated via a moving average). This ensures that while the features adapt to the new modality, the underlying grouping structure remains consistent with the global consensus observed so far.

## Expected Contribution
We aim to introduce a novel paradigm for Continual Multi-view Clustering by being the first to formally apply Domain Adaptation principles to this setting. Theoretically, this work will demonstrate that maintaining **structural consistency** (via similarity matrices) is a viable and privacy-preserving alternative to data replay for mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Practically, our proposed noise-weighting mechanism is expected to significantly enhance robustness against low-quality or noisy views in sequential learning environments.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated the performance of our proposed method (AdaptCMVC) against state-of-the-art baselines on clustering tasks involving incrementally available views.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **E-MNIST:** Image dataset based on MNIST. 70,000 handwritten digits (0-9). Two views: Original version and Edge-detection version.
    *   **E-FMNIST:** Fashion dataset with 10 classes of clothing items. 70,000 images ($32 \times 32$ pixels). Two views: Original version and Edge-detected version.
    *   **COIL-100:** 100 objects captured from various angles. Three views generated from RGB and grayscale images.
    *   **COIL-20:** 20 objects captured from various angles. Three views generated from RGB and grayscale images.
    *   **Office-31:** Office setting dataset with 2,253 items from 31 categories. Three views constructed by applying ColorJitter.
    *   **PatchedMNIST:** Subset of MNIST with 3 classes. Designed for large numbers of views. Images divided into $12 \times 7 \times 7$ non-overlapping patches; the 6 center patches were used as 6 distinct views.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **ACC:** Accuracy.
    *   **NMI:** Normalized Mutual Information.
    *   We reported average values and variance over 10 training runs.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Single-view clustering:** Joint-VAE, $\beta$-VAE (reported results for the best performing individual view).
    *   **Deep Multi-view Clustering (DMVC):** Multi-level Feature Learning for contrastive multi-View Clustering (MFLVC), End-to-end Adversarial attention network for Multi-modal Clustering (EAMC), CONtrAstive fusion Networks for multi-view clustering (CONAN), Global and Cross-view Feature Aggregation for multi-view clustering (GCFAgg), Multi-VAE.
    *   **Continual Multi-view Clustering (CMVC):** CMVC (method name), Continual Action Clustering with incremental views (CAC).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Framework:** PyTorch.
    *   **Training:** 50 epochs per session.
    *   **Optimizer:** Adam.
    *   **Batch Size:** 256.
    *   **Learning Rate:** $1 \times 10^{-4}$.
    *   **Model Selection:** We selected the epoch resulting in the lowest unsupervised training loss ($\mathcal{L}_c + \mathcal{L}_s + \mathcal{L}_r$).
    *   **Architecture:** Convolutional networks for encoder and decoder (symmetric structure).
    *   **Augmentations:** Random horizontal flipping, color jitter, Gaussian blur, and addition of Gaussian noise.
    *   **Ablation Configurations:** We tested the model without the structure alignment loss ($\mathcal{L}_s$) and without the noise robust consistency loss ($\mathcal{L}_c$).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Adaptation Process Performance:** We observed that AdaptCMVC steadily improves accuracy as the number of views increases (tested on PatchedMNIST up to 6 views). In contrast, the performance of baseline CMVC methods (CAC and CMVC) stagnated or improved much more slowly as the number of views increased.
*   **Comparison to Full-View Methods:** The final performance of AdaptCMVC on PatchedMNIST reached or exceeded the performance of the top traditional MVC baseline (GCFAgg), despite GCFAgg having simultaneous access to all views and AdaptCMVC only accessing them sequentially.
*   **Informative Views:** We noted that single highly informative views did not necessarily lead to immediate performance jumps for the sequential model (e.g., the introduction of View 4 in PatchedMNIST), yet the model continued to accumulate knowledge effectively over the long term.
*   **Robustness to View Order:** We observed that AdaptCMVC consistently outperformed other CMVC methods regardless of the order in which views were presented (tested on E-MNIST with View 1 $\rightarrow$ View 2 and View 2 $\rightarrow$ View 1).
*   **Ablation Findings:** The full AdaptCMVC model consistently outperformed the ablated versions (without $\mathcal{L}_s$ or without $\mathcal{L}_c$) across all tested datasets.
*   **Component Contribution:** We observed that the impact of specific loss components varied by dataset. For example, on some datasets, noise robustness ($\mathcal{L}_c$) was more critical, while on others, structure alignment ($\mathcal{L}_s$) played a larger role.
*   **Catastrophic Forgetting:** Analysis showed that the final model, after training on all views, retained strong performance on early views. In several cases (View 1, View 5, View 6 of PatchedMNIST), the final model outperformed a base model trained exclusively on that specific view, indicating successful backward transfer and knowledge preservation.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.

Instead use

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Traditional Multi-View Clustering (MVC) algorithms operate under the assumption that all views are available simultaneously for processing. However, in many real-world scenarios—such as medical diagnostics involving sequential imaging modalities or federated learning on edge devices—data accumulates incrementally over time. This setting, known as Continual Multi-view Clustering (CMVC), presents distinct challenges: views arrive sequentially, feature spaces evolve continuously, and access to historical raw data is prohibited due to storage or privacy constraints.

Current CMVC approaches predominantly rely on late fusion strategies, training individual models for each view and averaging partition matrices. These methods suffer from two critical failures:
1.  **View Discrepancy and Noise:** They fail to adapt effectively to significant feature shifts between views and are highly susceptible to view-specific noise.
2.  **Catastrophic Forgetting:** As the model adapts to new views without access to prior data, it loses the clustering structure learned from earlier sessions.

We aim to resolve these issues by moving away from simple late fusion and redefining CMVC through the lens of **Domain Adaptation**.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve robust CMVC by treating the sequential arrival of views as a domain adaptation problem. We propose a novel architecture, **AdaptCMVC**, which utilizes a **self-training framework** to adapt a base model to incoming views.

Our core technical hypothesis rests on two mechanisms:
1.  **Noise-Robust Self-Training:** By employing a teacher-student architecture with a weighted consistency loss, we can filter out noisy samples in new views based on their distance from previously learned prototypes.
2.  **Structure Alignment:** By maintaining and aligning a global similarity matrix structure rather than raw data, we can enforce consistency across views and prevent catastrophic forgetting without violating data privacy.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Problem Definition
We define the CMVC task as a sequence of $V$ clustering sessions $\{ S ^ { 0 } , S ^ { 1 } , \ldots , S ^ { V } \}$. Each session $v$ consists of $n$ unlabeled samples $\mathbf { X } ^ { v } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times d }$, where $d$ is the feature dimension. Critically, only $\mathbf { X } ^ { v }$ is accessible during session $v$. We must integrate knowledge from the current view with preserved knowledge from inaccessible previous views.

### 2. Base Model Construction (Session $v=0$)
In the initial session, we will establish a robust base feature extraction model using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). To enhance noise robustness, we will employ a masking strategy that randomly blurs pixels of the input $\mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v }$, resulting in a masked version $\mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v \prime }$.

The encoder $E _ { \phi } ( \cdot )$ with parameters $\phi$ will infer the approximate posterior of the latent representation $\mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v }$:
$$ q _ { \phi } ( \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } | \mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v \prime } ) = \mathcal { N } ( \mu ^ { v } , \sigma ^ { v 2 } ) $$
where $\mu ^ { v }$ and $\sigma ^ { v }$ are neural network outputs. We will apply the reparameterization trick:
$$ \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } = \mu ^ { v } + \sigma ^ { v } \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal { N } ( \mathbf { 0 } , \mathbf { I } ) $$

The decoder $D _ { \theta } ( \cdot )$ with parameters $\theta$ will reconstruct the original input:
$$ \hat { \mathbf { x } } _ { i } ^ { v } = p _ { \theta } ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v } \mid \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } ) $$

The training objective for the base model is the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO):
$$ \mathcal { L } _ { r } = \mathbb { E } _ { q _ { \phi } ( \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } \mid \mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v \prime } ) } [ \log p _ { \theta } ( \mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v } \mid \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } ) ] - K L ( q _ { \phi } ( \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } | \mathbf { x } _ { i } ^ { v \prime } ) \| p ( \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } ) ) $$
where $p ( \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } ) \sim \mathcal { N } ( \mathbf { 0 } , \mathbf { I } )$ is the standard Gaussian prior.

### 3. Noise-Robust Self-Training Framework (Incremental Sessions $v > 0$)
To handle view discrepancy, we will implement a student-teacher framework. The student model $f_{\psi}$ (initialized from the base model) learns from a teacher model $f_{\psi'}$.

**Teacher Model Update:**
The teacher parameters $\psi'$ will not be updated via gradient descent but via an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the student parameters to ensure stability:
$$ \psi _ { t } ^ { \prime } = \alpha \psi _ { t - 1 } ^ { \prime } + ( 1 - \alpha ) \psi _ { t } $$
where $\alpha$ is a smoothing factor and $t$ is the time step.

**Noise-Robust Consistency Loss:**
Standard consistency losses fail when new views contain noise. We will propose a weighted consistency loss that down-weights samples that are far from the class prototypes learned in the *previous* session.

Let $\mathbf { B } ^ { v - 1 } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { k \times d }$ be the class prototypes and $\mathbf { H } ^ { v - 1 }$ be the soft cluster assignments from session $v-1$. We calculate the distance $l ( i , b _ { i } ^ { v - 1 } )$ between the current sample representation $\mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v }$ and its corresponding previous prototype:
$$ l ( i , b _ { i } ^ { v - 1 } ) = \| \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } - \mathbf { h } _ { i } ^ { v - 1 } \mathbf { B } ^ { v - 1 } \| ^ { 2 } $$

The consistency loss $\mathcal { L } _ { c }$ forces the student's distribution $p ( \mathbf { z } _ { i d } ^ { v } )$ to match the teacher's distribution $p ( \mathbf { z } _ { i d } ^ { v \prime } )$ (derived from augmented inputs), weighted by the inverse distance to the prototype:
$$ \mathcal { L } _ { c } ( \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } ) = - \frac { 1 } { ( l ( i , b _ { i } ^ { v - 1 } ) ) ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { d } p ( \mathbf { z } _ { i d } ^ { v } ) \log p ( \mathbf { z } _ { i d } ^ { v \prime } ) $$

This mechanism ensures that the model adaption is driven by reliable samples consistent with established clusters, rather than outliers or noise.

### 4. Structure Alignment Learning
To prevent catastrophic forgetting, we will enforce global structural consistency without accessing $\mathbf { X } ^ { v - 1 }$. We will maintain a similarity matrix $\mathbf { S } ^ { v - 1 }$ representing the group structure of the previous session.

**Initialization:**
At the start of session $v$, $\mathbf { S } ^ { v - 1 }$ is initialized using the previous cluster assignments $\mathbf { H } ^ { v - 1 }$:
$$ \mathbf { s } _ { i j } ^ { v - 1 } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { \mathbf { h } _ { i k } ^ { v - 1 } \neq \mathbf { h } _ { j k } ^ { v - 1 } } \\ { 1 } & { \mathbf { h } _ { i k } ^ { v - 1 } = \mathbf { h } _ { j k } ^ { v - 1 } } \end{array} \right. $$

**Alignment Loss:**
We define the current view's pairwise cosine similarity matrix $\mathbf { C } ^ { v }$ where $c _ { i j } ^ { v } = \frac { < \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } , \mathbf { z } _ { j } ^ { v } > } { \| \mathbf { z } _ { i } ^ { v } \| \| \mathbf { z } _ { j } ^ { v } \| }$. The structure alignment loss is the Mean Squared Error between the preserved structure and the current structure:
$$ \mathcal { L } _ { s } = \frac { 1 } { n ^ { 2 } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \| \mathbf { s } _ { i j } ^ { v - 1 } - \mathbf { c } _ { i j } ^ { v } \| $$

**Structure Update:**
During the session, the global structure matrix is updated via a moving average to gradually incorporate new structural information:
$$ \mathbf { S } _ { t } ^ { v - 1 } = \beta \mathbf { S } _ { t - 1 } ^ { v - 1 } + ( 1 - \beta ) \mathbf { C } _ { t } ^ { v } $$

### 5. Final Optimization Objective
The complete objective function for the student model in incremental sessions will be the weighted sum of the reconstruction loss (adapted for the current view), the noise-robust consistency loss, and the structure alignment loss:
$$ \mathcal { L } _{total} = \mathcal { L } _ { r } + \mathcal { L } _ { c } + \mathcal { L } _ { s } $$

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework Innovation:** We will introduce the first method to explicitly model Continual Multi-view Clustering as a domain adaptation problem, offering a more theoretically grounded approach than existing late-fusion heuristics.
2.  **Noise Robustness:** The proposed inverse-distance weighted consistency loss will provide a specific mechanism to mitigate the negative transfer caused by noisy samples in incremental views.
3.  **Forgetting Mitigation:** The structure alignment mechanism will allow the model to retain global group structures across sessions without violating data privacy protocols (i.e., without storing raw historical data), solving the catastrophic forgetting problem inherent in sequential learning.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
